newsitem.title: UK: UK seeks not-for-profit lottery operator.
newsitem.headline: UK seeks not-for-profit lottery operator.

text.p: The government on Monday said it was seeking an operator to run Britain's national lottery on an efficient not-for-profit basis.

In a policy white paper, Culture, Media and Sport Secretary Chris Smith said he would welcome proposals as to how to achieve the government's twin objective of maximising the return to good causes, while "removing unnecessary profit margins".
"We do not intend to prescribe the nature of the operator," Smith said.

Labour, unhappy at the handsome profits made by lottery operator Camelot, said in its manifesto for the May 1 election that it would "seek an efficient not-for-profit operator to ensure that the maximum sums go to good causes".

Camelot, whose licence expires in 2001, is a consortium owned by Cadbury Schweppes Plc, GTECH Holdings Corp, De La Rue Plc and Racal Electronics Plc, which each have a 22.5 percent stake, and Japan's Fujitsu, which owns a 10 percent stake.

In the white paper, Smith acknowledged that the operating expenses of Britain's lottery were much lower than the international average and said the government wanted to harness the expertise of the private sector.
He said he expected the licence to be put out to competitive tender, with the bidders judged on the following criteria:
-- their ability to maximise returns to good causes.
-- their ability to run the lottery efficiently and to provide the best value for money.
-- the financial viability and sustainability of their plans.
-- the transparency of the operation. The amount and nature of the returns to the operator must be reasonable, related to performance and easily understood.
The paper said the different types of operator would each have the opportunity to show how they could meet these criteria.
In said models might include:
-- a single company made up of a consortium of suppliers.
-- a holding company that contracts out individual services.
-- a multi-purpose company that is able to use the lottery network for other activities, thus reducing the management fee required and leaving more money for good causes.
-- an organisation where the distribution of profits is not to shareholders but to employees and the good causes.
Smith proposed that the lottery's director general should choose the new operator with the help of a panel with expertise in business, including the lottery market.
He also proposed giving the regulator powers to impose financial penalties on the operator in the event of serious licence breaches.

The white paper confirmed the government's plans to channel one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) of lottery proceeds to a New Opportunities Fund and to a new National Endowment for Science, Technology and the Arts (NESTA).
The New Opportunities Fund will spend money on health, education and, subsequently, the environment.
Its first three initiatives will have the target to deliver, by 2001, the following:
-- training and support for Britain's 500,000 serving teachers in the use of information and communications technology, plus training for some 10,000 library staff.
-- out-of-school activities, including homework, involving at least half of all secondary schools and a quarter of primary schools.
-- a core network of healthy living centres.
($ = 0.595 British Pounds)
